newsitem.title: JAPAN: Israeli foreign minister says housing for peace.
newsitem.headline: Israeli foreign minister says housing for peace.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Friday brushed aside growing international criticism of his government's decision to build houses for Jewish settlers in Arab East Jerusalem.
Levy, in Tokyo on a five-day visit which began on Wednesday, said the plan to build housing for the settlers as well as for the Arab population was an attempt to foster a spirit of coexistence.
"I am filled with pride that the Israeli cabinet decided to build 3,500 housing units for the Arab population," Levy told a news conference in Tokyo.
"I am hopeful that the two populations living together will enhance the possibility of coexistence," he said.
On Wednesday, Israel's ministerial committee on Jerusalem approved the building of 6,500 homes for Jews and more than 3,000 houses for Arabs in East Jerusalem.
The decision sparked international criticism, joined by the United States and Japan, and triggered Palestinian warnings that the plan could unleash bloodshed.
On Thursday, Levy met Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda for talks on bilateral issues and the Middle East peace process.
Both Hashimoto and Ikeda criticised Israel's housing decision. Hashimoto said the move was a "negative element" in the peace process.
Levy said a majority of land to be used for the new houses was privately owned by Jews.
He said Arabs and the international community should not see a crisis in every small turn because this would endanger the entire Middle East peace process.
"I don't believe this is a make-or-break issue," Levy said.

Asked if Japan's latest criticism affected bilateral ties, Levy said Japan was not being critical of Israel and that his meetings with Hashimoto and Ikeda were conducted in a positive atmosphere. "Let me stress, the talks were good and friendly," Levy told reporters.
Earlier on Friday, Levy also asked Japanese business leaders to boost investment in Israel.
In a lecture to Japanese executives, Levy encouraged Japanese firms to set up businesses in Israel, boasting that his country offered abundant opportunities in high technology and agriculture.
Levy also said a mission of Israeli business executives as well Israel's finance and trade ministers would visit Japan in April to discuss various business opportunities.
"Israel doesn't need aid. We want to do business," Levy told the Japanese executives.
Hashimoto and Levy agreed to hold more talks on trade, joint ventures and technology development.

Levy also urged the Japanese government to resume talks on allowing direct flights from Israel to Japan. The talks lapsed two years ago after Japan expressed security concerns regarding direct flights from Tel Aviv.
Ikeda told Levy on Thursday that aviation specialists would study the issue.
